v.q: In cache-aside, what should the application do after updating a row in the database?
o: Delete the cached key so the next read reloads it
Write the new value into the cache and keep the old TTL untouched forever
Delete the key before the database write so nothing stale remains
Flush the whole Redis instance to be safe
v.w: Delete after the database write: the next read rebuilds from the source of truth. Updating in place can let an older writer store last, and deleting before the write lets a reader reload the old value.

v.q: Which statement about cache-aside is NOT true?
o: The cache is updated before the database write
The app reads the cache first
On a miss the app loads from the database
The key is deleted after a write
v.w: Delete after the database commit. Writing the cache first can leave a stale value if the database write fails.

v.q: What is the difference between expiry and eviction in Redis?
o: Expiry removes keys whose TTL ended; eviction removes valid keys when maxmemory is reached
Expiry removes least used keys; eviction removes keys that are too large
They are the same mechanism with two names for different Redis versions
Expiry happens only on replicas; eviction happens only on the primary node
v.w: Expiry is about time (TTL), eviction is about space (maxmemory and maxmemory-policy). Both can delete a key, for different reasons.

v.q: Which Redis feature removes a key because its TTL ended?
o: Expiry
Eviction
Replication
Persistence
v.w: Expiry is time-based. Eviction frees memory by removing valid keys when maxmemory is reached.

v.q: What does Redis do by default (noeviction) when maxmemory is reached?
o: Rejects write commands with an out-of-memory error while reads keep working
Evicts the least recently used key from the whole key space
Evicts keys with the nearest expiry first until memory is free
Stops serving all commands until an operator frees memory by hand
v.w: noeviction is the default: writes fail with an OOM error. For a cache, set allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu so cold keys are discarded instead.

v.q: Which policy lets Redis remove the least recently used key from all keys when memory is full?
o: allkeys-lru
noeviction
volatile-ttl
allkeys-never
v.w: allkeys-lru evicts across the whole key space. noeviction rejects writes instead.

v.q: A very popular key expires and a thousand requests hit the database at once. What is this called and what prevents it?
o: Cache stampede; let one request rebuild the value using a lock or sync = true
Cache penetration; cache a null marker for the missing key
Cache avalanche; switch the eviction policy to allkeys-random
Big key problem; split the value into smaller hashes
v.w: A stampede (thundering herd) is concurrent rebuilds of one hot key. Single-flight locking, refresh-ahead or serving stale while one request refreshes prevent it.

v.q: Which defence fits many requests rebuilding one expired hot key together?
o: A lock so one request rebuilds it
A longer client timeout
More Redis replicas
A smaller maxmemory
v.w: One request refreshes the value while the others wait or use the old one.

v.q: Requests keep arriving for account ids that do not exist, so every one reaches the database. Which defence fits best?
o: Cache a short-lived null marker and put a Bloom filter of valid ids in front
Raise the TTL of every existing key to one week
Enable AOF persistence with fsync always
Use Redis Cluster so the misses spread over more nodes
v.w: This is cache penetration: nothing exists to cache. A null marker with a short TTL, input validation and a Bloom filter reject impossible ids early.

v.q: Which defence is NOT useful against requests for ids that do not exist?
o: Raising the TTL of existing keys
Caching a null marker
A Bloom filter of valid ids
Validating the id format
v.w: Longer TTLs do not help, because the misses are for keys that were never cached.

v.q: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs?
o: So keys loaded together do not all expire together and cause an avalanche
So Redis can evict them in a faster order
So replicas stay in sync with the primary clock
So that LFU counters are reset at different times
v.w: Identical TTLs on keys loaded together make them expire at the same instant, sending the whole load to the database. Jitter spreads the expiry over time.

v.q: Many keys cached at startup all expire at the same second. What is this risk called?
o: Cache avalanche
Cache penetration
Hot key
Slow log
v.w: Random jitter on the TTLs spreads the expiry over time.

v.q: Why is KEYS * discouraged on a production Redis?
o: It scans the whole key space in one blocking call, freezing the single command thread
It returns only keys without a TTL, giving misleading results
It deletes expired keys as a side effect and so slows reads
It is not available in Redis Cluster and returns an error
v.w: Redis runs commands on one thread, so a slow command blocks every client. Use SCAN, which iterates in small cursor-based steps.

v.q: Which Redis command is a safe way to iterate keys in production?
o: SCAN
KEYS *
FLUSHALL
DEBUG SLEEP
v.w: SCAN returns small batches with a cursor, so the single command thread is not blocked for long.

v.q: In Redis Cluster, how does a client reach the right node for a key?
o: The key maps to one of 16,384 hash slots, each owned by a primary
The client asks Sentinel which node holds the key each time
Keys are copied to every node and any node can answer
The node is chosen by the key's TTL and the data type
v.w: Slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. Related keys can share a slot through hash tags such as {user42}:cart, which multi-key commands require.

v.q: Which statement about Redis Cluster is NOT true?
o: Every key is copied to all nodes
There are 16,384 hash slots
Each slot belongs to one primary
Clients follow redirects
v.w: Keys are partitioned across primaries. Replicas hold copies of a single primary.
